title: Basepoint change and homotopy invariance of homotopy groups
statement:
Let $I=[0,1]$ with its usual topology. For a topological space $T$ let $\pi_0(T)$ be its set of path components and, for $n\geq1$ and $t\in T$, let $\pi_n(T,t)$ be the group of continuous maps $(I^n,\partial I^n)\to(T,t)$ modulo homotopy fixed on the boundary, with concatenation in the first coordinate. A continuous map induces maps on these sets and groups by postcomposition. For a path $\gamma:I\to T$ from $t_0$ to $t_1$, define $\beta_\gamma:\pi_n(T,t_1)\to\pi_n(T,t_0)$ as follows: for a representative $a$, put $r(u)=2\max_i|u_i-\tfrac12|$ and represent $\beta_\gamma[a]$ by $a(2u-\tfrac12)$ on $r(u)\leq\tfrac12$ and by $\gamma(2-2r(u))$ on $r(u)\geq\tfrac12$. This defines a group isomorphism, with inverse induced by $\overline\gamma(s)=\gamma(1-s)$.

Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces and $H:I\times X\to Y$ a continuous homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$, where $f_i(x)=H(i,x)$. The two induced functions $\pi_0(X)\to\pi_0(Y)$ coincide. For every $x\in X$ and $n\geq1$, writing $\gamma_x(s)=H(s,x)$, one has
$$\beta_{\gamma_x}\circ(f_1)_*=(f_0)_*:\pi_n(X,x)\longrightarrow\pi_n(Y,f_0(x)).$$
Consequently $f_0$ induces a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on every homotopy group at every source basepoint if and only if $f_1$ does. Every homotopy equivalence $f:X\to Y$, meaning a continuous map admitting a continuous inverse up to continuous homotopies with the identities, induces such a bijection and such isomorphisms. No connectedness or stationary-basepoint condition on the homotopies is imposed. In particular, if two maps of simplicial sets have continuously homotopic geometric realizations, then one is a weak homotopy equivalence in the sense of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] if and only if the other is.

source.place: Allen Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Section 4.1, Definitions and Basic Constructions, printed pp. 340–342 (cube model, change-of-basepoint isomorphisms, functoriality and unbased homotopy equivalences); Exercise 4.1.2, printed p. 358. The displayed shell is the explicit concentric-cube construction on p. 341; the homotopy identity uses the same moving-boundary construction. No Stacks tag states this topological result.

proof.text: Put $D=I^n$, $c=(\tfrac12,\ldots,\tfrac12)$ and $r(u)=2\max_i|u_i-\tfrac12|$. Thus $0\leq r\leq1$, and $r(u)=1$ exactly on $\partial D$. We will paste formulas on two closed subsets covering a cube or a product of cubes. This pasting rule follows directly from continuity: for a closed set $C$ in the target, each branch has closed inverse image in its closed domain, hence in the whole domain, and the inverse image under the pasted map is their finite union. All the rescalings below have positive scale at least $\tfrac12$. A rescaled coordinate can be extended continuously off its prescribed region using $q(v)=\max(0,\min(1,v))$; thus the branch formulas are restrictions of continuous maps, including at parameter endpoints.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 340–341, cube and concentric-shell construction; elementary continuity details supplied here.

proof.text: For a path $\gamma:t_0\leadsto t_1$ and a representative $a:(D,\partial D)\to(T,t_1)$, paste $a(c+2(u-c))$ on $r\leq\tfrac12$ and $\gamma(2-2r)$ on $r\geq\tfrac12$. At the seam the rescaled point is on $\partial D$ and both values are $t_1$; at $r=1$ the value is $t_0$. Step 1 proves continuity. If $a$ is replaced through a boundary-fixed homotopy $a_v$, the same formula with $a_v$ in the inner cube is a boundary-fixed homotopy of the pasted maps. Hence this is precisely the well-defined function $\beta_\gamma$ on homotopy classes in the statement. Postcomposition by a continuous map preserves boundary-fixed homotopies and concatenations pointwise, so the induced maps are well-defined homomorphisms, preserve identities and compose strictly as functions on classes.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341, change-of-basepoint construction and homotopies of its inputs; p. 342, functoriality.

proof.text: Here is an explicit calculation to be used in subsequent steps. Suppose $F:I\times D\to T$ is continuous and $F(t,u)=\gamma(t)$ for every $u\in\partial D$. Set $\lambda(t)=1-t/2$. On $r(u)\leq\lambda(t)$ put $B(t,u)=F(t,c+(u-c)/\lambda(t))$; on $r(u)\geq\lambda(t)$ put $B(t,u)=\gamma(2-2r(u))$. The regions are closed and cover $I\times D$. On their intersection the normalized point is on $\partial D$ and $2-2r=t$, so both formulas give $\gamma(t)$. On the outer region $0\leq2-2r\leq t\leq1$, so its path argument is in $I$. Step 1, using the clamped coordinate extensions there and the extension $\gamma(\min(1,2-2r))$ for the outer branch, proves joint continuity.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342; explicit agent expansion of the moving-boundary collar calculation underlying the nonstationary-basepoint assertion.

proof.text: The formula in step 3 gives $B(0,u)=F(0,u)$, $B(1,u)=\beta_\gamma(F(1,-))(u)$, and $B(t,u)=\gamma(0)$ on $\partial D$. Consequently $[F(0,-)]=\beta_\gamma[F(1,-)]$ as homotopy classes based at $\gamma(0)$. This calculation uses only substitution into the displayed formula and the definition of boundary-fixed homotopy; it does not assume that $\beta_\gamma$ is invertible or multiplicative.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342; endpoints of the explicit moving-boundary collar calculation in step 3.

proof.text: For a representative $a:(D,\partial D)\to(T,t_1)$ construct a sweep in the opposite direction. Set $\mu(s)=(1+s)/2$. On $r\leq\mu(s)$ put $A(s,u)=a(c+(u-c)/\mu(s))$, and on $r\geq\mu(s)$ put $A(s,u)=\gamma(s+2-2r)$. On the outer region $s\leq s+2-2r\leq1$; at the seam the path argument is $1$ and the inner point is on $\partial D$, so both values are $t_1$. The two closed regions therefore paste continuously by step 1, with outer extension $\gamma(\min(1,s+2-2r))$.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341, varying the concentric cube; explicit agent formula for a sweep with moving boundary.

proof.text: Substitution in step 5 gives $A(0,-)=\beta_\gamma a$, $A(1,-)=a$, and $A(s,u)=\gamma(s)$ for $u\in\partial D$. The scale $\mu$ never vanishes. In particular these equalities hold also at $s=1,r=1$: both branches are $t_1$. Thus the sweep is an ordinary homotopy whose entire boundary follows the prescribed path, with the stated exact endpoint maps.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341; endpoint and boundary verification for step 5.

proof.text: Apply the identity of step 4 to the reversed sweep $F(t,u)=A(1-t,u)$, whose boundary path is $\overline\gamma(t)=\gamma(1-t)$. Its endpoints give $[a]=\beta_{\overline\gamma}(\beta_\gamma[a])$. For a representative $b:(D,\partial D)\to(T,t_0)$, steps 5–6 with path $\overline\gamma$ give a continuous sweep $A_b$ with $A_b(0,-)=\beta_{\overline\gamma}b$, $A_b(1,-)=b$, and boundary value $\overline\gamma(s)$. Its reversal $G(t,u)=A_b(1-t,u)$ has endpoints $b$ and $\beta_{\overline\gamma}b$ and boundary $\overline\gamma(1-t)=\gamma(t)$. Step 4 applied to $G$ gives $[b]=\beta_\gamma(\beta_{\overline\gamma}[b])$. Therefore the two shell maps are inverse bijections. No contraction of a loop in $T$ is assumed.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342, inverse change-of-basepoint map; explicit proof using steps 4–6 instead of suppressed reparametrizations.

proof.text: For representatives $a,b$ based at $t_1$, take their sweeps $A_a,A_b$ from steps 5–6 and concatenate in the first cube coordinate: $C(s,u)=A_a(s,(2u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n))$ for $u_1\leq\tfrac12$ and $C(s,u)=A_b(s,(2u_1-1,u_2,\ldots,u_n))$ for $u_1\geq\tfrac12$. At the middle face both values are $\gamma(s)$, proving continuity by step 1. The outer boundary also has value $\gamma(s)$. At $s=0$ this is $(\beta_\gamma a)*(\beta_\gamma b)$ and at $s=1$ it is $a*b$. Step 4 applied to $C$ therefore gives $\beta_\gamma([a][b])=(\beta_\gamma[a])(\beta_\gamma[b])$. Along with step 7 this makes $\beta_\gamma$ a group isomorphism with exactly the specified inverse. The calculation preserves the order of the two factors and applies unchanged when $n=1$.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 341, property (1) of change of basepoint; explicit alternative using the moving-boundary calculation.

proof.text: For the given $H:I\times X\to Y$ and a representative $a:(D,\partial D)\to(X,x)$, set $F(t,u)=H(t,a(u))$. Its boundary is $\gamma_x(t)=H(t,x)$. Step 4 gives $[(f_0\circ a)]=\beta_{\gamma_x}[(f_1\circ a)]$, the asserted identity of induced homomorphisms for every class. On path components, $t\mapsto H(t,x)$ itself is a path from $f_0(x)$ to $f_1(x)$, so their classes coincide for every $x$. Postcomposition sends paths to paths, so this is an equality of the induced functions on $\pi_0$.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342, homotopy invariance and the nonstationary-basepoint assertion; moving-boundary details supplied in steps 3–4.

proof.text: For each source basepoint and positive degree the two induced maps in step 9 differ by the group isomorphism $\beta_{\gamma_x}$ of step 8. One is therefore an isomorphism exactly when the other is. The component functions are equal, so one is bijective exactly when the other is. Quantifying over all source basepoints and all $n\geq1$ gives the claimed equivalence of the two weak-homotopy-equivalence conditions.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342; elementary consequence of the explicit identity in step 9.

proof.text: Let $g$ be a homotopy inverse of $f$. By step 9 and the strict functoriality in step 2, the induced functions on components of $g$ and $f$ are mutual inverses. Fix $x\in X$ and $n\geq1$, and write $p=f_{*,x}$, $q=g_{*,f(x)}$ and $v=f_{*,g(f(x))}$. The homotopy $gf\simeq1_X$, evaluated at $x$, together with steps 8–9 says $qp:\pi_n(X,x)\to\pi_n(X,g(f(x)))$ is an isomorphism. The homotopy $fg\simeq1_Y$, evaluated at $f(x)$, says $vq:\pi_n(Y,f(x))\to\pi_n(Y,f(g(f(x))))$ is an isomorphism. Surjectivity of $qp$ makes $q$ surjective, and injectivity of $vq$ makes $q$ injective. Thus $q$ is an isomorphism and $p=q^{-1}(qp)$ is an isomorphism. This proves the conclusion for $f$ without requiring the inverse homotopies to fix a point or satisfy triangle identities. If the spaces are empty the component argument still applies and the based assertions are vacuous.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342, paragraph before Proposition 4.1; Exercise 2 on printed p. 358. Explicit algebra at the three possibly different basepoints.

proof.text: For maps of simplicial sets whose realizations are continuously homotopic, apply step 10 to their realization maps. The definition in [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] says that a weak homotopy equivalence is exactly a map whose realization is bijective on path components and isomorphic on every positive homotopy group at every basepoint. Hence the two simplicial maps satisfy that condition simultaneously. Only this defining sentence of the cited node is used; no model-structure existence or right-properness assertion is used.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342, followed by the realization-based definition in lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper.
